title: Venice’s historic buildings face mounting pressures. Could drones and digital twins help protect them?
content: With its canals, bridges and historic buildings, Venice has an extraordinary architectural legacy. But preserving many of its most treasured monuments presents a growing challenge. In recent years, floods have damaged historic structures across the city, including the iconic St. Mark’s Basilica and other UNESCO World Heritage sites. Venice’s lagoon environment presents challenges for the preservation of historic buildings. Persistent moisture and salt can gradually weaken stonework and mortar, while the city’s complex foundations and the age of its structures can create additional vulnerabilities. But innovative technologies could help detect signs of damage and aging earlier, to protect the city’s heritage before it is damaged irreparably. For centuries, the Church of San Francesco della Vigna has been part of Venice’s remarkable architectural landscape. Its distinctive façade, designed by Renaissance architect Andrea Palladio, and its bell tower are among the defining features of a historic complex. A recent survey employed digital methods, including drone photography and terrestrial laser scanning, to capture the church’s architecture in three dimensions. Researchers have combined that digital documentation with archival research and structural analysis, creating a detailed model that can help identify vulnerable areas and support future conservation work. “These tools transformed how engineers, architects, and restorers interact with the monument,” said Ilaria Forti, the architect leading the project, who also teaches in the restoration, survey and digital drawing laboratory at the University Iuav of Venice. The church was designed by Italian Renaissance architect Jacopo Sansovino and completed in 1554, with a façade added later by Palladio. After specialists found parts of the façade at risk of detaching in the 1990s, it was stabilized and restored. Yet visible damage tells only part of the story of a building’s condition. Understanding how its materials and structure are aging, and identifying areas that may need attention, are essential to planning future conservation, Forti told CNN. Forti’s work at San Francesco della Vigna followed an earlier conservation project at another Venetian church, Santa Maria di Nazareth, near the city’s railway station. From 2015 to 2022 Forti led restoration work on its Baroque façade, where the Carrara marble had deteriorated under the effects of the lagoon environment. After completing the restoration, Forti approached the University Iuav of Venice to develop a monitoring program. This led to a collaboration with its VIDE Lab, directed by Professor Giuseppe D’Acunto and operated by research fellow and engineer Irene Rocca. The experience provided a foundation for the project at San Francesco della Vigna, which began in 2023. This time, the researchers wanted to document the building’s condition before further conservation work began, rather than monitoring the results of an intervention that had already taken place. “The order of the Franciscan friars asked us to run a monitoring campaign,” Forti said. “And so it was a perfect timing to combine our research.” The work was supported by the Venice in Peril Fund, following the interest shown by the Association of International Private Committees for the Safeguarding of Venice. “Traditional inspection methods, like ground-based visual checks or limited scaffolding, often miss micro-fissures, structural shifts in high-altitude zones, and internal material failures,” Forti said. Drone photography allowed researchers to reach areas of the façade and bell tower that would be difficult to inspect from the ground. But flying the drones in Venice brought an unexpected challenge. “There’s so many seagulls around. And they really took these drones as a threat,” said Jonathan Hoyte, a climbing restorer who carried out inspections and repairs using rope-access techniques. “Sometimes you couldn’t even fly them because they’d start trying to attack the drones. So it wasn’t so simple.” Photogrammetry, using overlapping photographs taken from different angles, was used to reconstruct the building’s surfaces in three dimensions. It was coupled with laser scanner technology that measures depth and distance directly, recording three-dimensional spatial coordinates. “Laser scanning is a technology that gives exactly the position of the point — in our case, the position of the façade, of the tower, of the statues, for example. And it also gives us their color, their texture,” Forti explained. The digital mapping helped identify areas where stonework had deteriorated under the effects of Venice’s lagoon climate. The models provided further information about cracks and areas where structural stresses could be concentrated, including around decorative statues, cornices, and other projecting features. By analyzing sections of the 3D model, the researchers found that the upper portion of the façade was leaning slightly. The team also used the model to assess the bell tower’s vulnerability to earthquakes, identifying potential structural weaknesses, including a tendency toward overturning. Debra Laefer, a professor at New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering, who was not involved in the project, said advances in remote-sensing technologies have changed how specialists document historic structures. “Moving to noncontact methods in the form of remote sensing, such as thermal, imaging, laser scanning, hyperspectral, has moved the field from point measurements to more holistic documentation,” she said. The survey data was only the starting point. The researchers combined the digital measurements with historical records, information about the building materials and structural assessments to create a more complete picture of the church. Using the 3D model as the base, the team built finite element modeling (FEM) — an engineering method that divides a structure into smaller parts to analyze numerically how it responds to forces and where stresses may concentrate. The method was used to investigate the structural behavior of complex features, including the church’s statues and other architectural elements. This information was then incorporated into a digital model that goes beyond a visual reconstruction of the building and contains information about areas of potential vulnerability. “Now we have a digital twin, and for the future, for the next generation, we can have a database, a place of support for possible future intervention,” Forti said. Luigi La Rocca, head of the Department for the Protection of Cultural Heritage (DiT) at Italy’s Ministry of Culture, agreed that monitoring technologies can reveal information that would not otherwise be detectable by a simple visual survey of the artifact. “Consider, for example, the data provided by sensors relating to the stresses and movements to which a structure is subjected,” he said. But creating a detailed digital record is only part of the process. Turning that information into practical conservation plans and 3D models requires the expertise of architects, engineers and specialists, said Aylin Orbasli, a professor at Oxford Brookes University’s School of Architecture, who wasn’t involved in the Venice project. The church’s façade is also distinguished by two monumental bronze statues depicting Moses and St. Paul, created by Tiziano Aspetti. Their intricate shapes made it particularly challenging for the team to produce accurate digital models. The researchers worked with statuary expert Professor Gabriella Liva at the LAR Lab, Iuav, to explore how other representations of Moses and Paul could help establish the geometry of the figures. Researcher Irene Rocca, under the supervision of Professor Anna Saetta at Iuav, used finite element analysis to examine how the bronze statue of Moses responds to its own weight. The analysis identified a concentration of stress around the ankle, where the supporting area narrows, but the calculated stress remained below the strength limits of the bronze. The digital survey method had practical benefits for the specialists working on the church. For Hoyte, whose company Extreme Woks uses rope-access techniques to monitor the building, having a scientific picture of its condition helped him determine which areas to inspect and how best to approach the work. “Knowing that to go here instead of there, it really saves time and energy to put the ropes exactly where they need to be,” he said. The drone survey also revealed vegetation growing in parts of the building that would have been difficult to reach. On the bell tower, the team even spotted blackberry bushes growing near the top. Hoyte and his colleagues treated the plants before returning several weeks later to remove them and their roots. They then used mortar to seal the joints where the vegetation had been growing. While photographs and 3D models can help identify areas that need attention, they cannot fully replace a close physical examination of the materials. “You might see cracks, but in order to understand if those cracks are completely at risk or not, you need to go and touch them,” Hoyte said. The researchers hope the digital reconstruction will become more than a record of the church’s current condition. Data showing how the building responds to events such as strong winds or earthquakes, for example, could eventually be incorporated. The idea is to ensure that future conservation specialists can build on the work already completed. “In conservation, I think it’s important not to start every time from zero,” said Rocca. “In this case, we have a lot of information, a lot of work already done.” Long-term monitoring can also help specialists determine how historic buildings respond to changing environmental conditions. “Longitudinal data,” Orbasli said, “can support our understanding of what is happening to the building fabric under different climatic conditions. This is becoming increasingly important with climate change.” But the technologies also bring practical challenges. Orbasli said the cost of the equipment, the volume of generated data and the computing power needed to process it can make their use difficult, particularly in regions with limited digital infrastructure. “It is by no means an equal playing field,” she said. Laefer identified further challenges in managing the large amounts of information generated by digital surveys, including preserving datasets for future comparison and combining information from different types of sensors. “The main limitations today are systematic data archiving, data processing, as the files can be very large, and combining multiple sensor outputs,” she said. La Rocca pointed to similar problems. The Ministry is trialing integrated monitoring, which brings together information from different technologies. “This methodology enables us to address scenarios characterized by multiple risks, even in the presence of differing environmental and cultural conditions,” La Rocca said. “The same technologies can also be used to carry out rapid damage assessments following emergency events.” What sets the San Francesco della Vigna project apart, Forti said, is the collaboration between different areas of expertise. Bringing together engineering, architectural conservation and historical research allows the team to look at the monument from different perspectives and build a more complete understanding of its condition. “The innovative part was to use them combined, all of them together, and to use them for the digital twin, and to use them for the assessment,” Forti said.

content: A newly identified prehistoric whale had unusual adaptations that may have allowed it to hunt along the seafloor millions of years ago. An ancient whale that lived millions of years ago had a skull so dramatically distorted that its face appeared pushed to one side. Its bony nostrils were displaced entirely to the left, and its oversized snout curved sharply downward. Scientists have identified the animal as Scaphokogia huachafo , an extinct pygmy sperm whale with the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a cetacean. The fossil dates to the Late Miocene, approximately 6.3 to 5.6 million years ago, and belonged to a whale measuring about 2.7 meters (8.9 feet) long. Researchers believe its skull may also represent the greatest facial asymmetry known in any mammal. Most vertebrates have skulls that are approximately symmetrical, with corresponding structures on either side of the head. Toothed whales are an exception. Their skulls have evolved asymmetrical shapes to accommodate specialized organs involved in producing sound and echolocation, allowing them to navigate and detect prey underwater. “Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo , this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked,” explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study. He investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich and is now an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU). The whale’s unusual anatomy suggests a feeding strategy very different from that of modern sperm whales, which pursue squid in deep ocean waters. Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have been adapted for searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal seas. Its thick, tubular snout contained dense bone and hardened cartilage that added weight toward the front of its body. The snout angled downward by 31 degrees, while reconstructions of the joint between the skull and first neck vertebra suggest the animal could lower its head by as much as 55 degrees. “The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom,” explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, study co-author and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich. “The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment.” Unlike some modern marine mammals that forage along the bottom, Scaphokogia lacked specialized facial whiskers and visual adaptations associated with locating prey in sediment. Researchers therefore suspect it relied on its unusually developed biosonar system to detect food hidden in soft seabed deposits. This remains a hypothesis based on its anatomy rather than direct evidence of its hunting behavior. Its specialized ecological niche apparently disappeared as ocean conditions changed near the end of the Miocene. The skull was recovered in the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru, a desert region famous for exceptionally preserved marine fossils. Benites-Palomino encountered the specimen in 2015 while working on his bachelor’s thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its extreme shape initially raised the possibility that geological forces had distorted the skull after the animal died. “The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy – that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years,” says Benites-Palomino. “But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.” The researchers chose a species name that reflects the animal’s unconventional appearance. Huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and describes something extravagant, flashy, bizarre, or aesthetically excessive. “In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant, or difficult to categorize aesthetically,” says Benites-Palomino. “When we looked at the proportions of this whale – with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout – it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.” Reference: “Extreme cranial asymmetry in extinct benthic feeding sperm whales” by Aldo Benites-Palomino, Marcelo R. Sánchez-Villagra, Florencia Paolucci, Jorge Vélez-Juarbe, Alberto Collareta, Apolline Alfsen, Alton Dooley, Dan Omura, Mario Urbina, Rodolfo Salas-Gismondi and Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, 9 November 2026, Communications Biology . DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-11074-2 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

title: Nvidia’s turmoil is prompting a rotation across chip stocks. Here's what we know
content: Nvidia 's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its biggest rivals, as investors bet that Jensen Huang's departure could loosen the AI chip giant's grip on an industry it has long dominated. From AMD to Broadcom and even partner TSMC , chipmakers are emerging as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval, with market watchers pointing to a possible redistribution of manufacturing capacity and a narrowing of Nvidia's technological lead. "What you're seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up," said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at Manulife Investment Management. That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang's resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs including with a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy . Huang's departure could give competitors an opportunity to close the gap as Nvidia navigates leadership uncertainty, Franklin highlighted, adding that the rotation was already helping fuel positive momentum in other semiconductor stocks. Farzin Azam, managing director of equities trading at Mizuho Americas, said the shift was evident on trading desks, with investors moving toward chipmakers less exposed to Nvidia's management turmoil. "Names such as TSMC, names such as Broadcom, names such as Advanced Micro will come as winners of this because they don't have this overhang of a management disruption," Azam told CNBC. Nvidia shares have plunged 11% so far this week, while rivals AMD and Broadcom have gained 30% and 24%, respectively. TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's most advanced processors, has also rallied 11% over the same period, as it stands to benefit , irrespective of which chip designer gains or loses. A rotation away from AI names perceived as risky also positions TSMC as a relatively safer play for those bullish on the overall theme. The rotation away from Nvidia has also extended into less speculative corners of the semiconductor industry, including analog chipmakers such as Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Infineon, as investors adopt a more defensive stance, he said. Texas Instruments has climbed about 13% this week, while Analog Devices and Germany's Infineon have advanced 12% and 14%, respectively. Beyond the immediate market reaction, Huang's exit could fundamentally reshape competition across the AI supply chain, according to Dylan Patel, chief executive at semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis. Patel said Huang had personally cultivated relationships with manufacturers and component suppliers, helping Nvidia secure scarce production capacity ahead of rivals. That advantage could now come under pressure as companies including Google and Amazon strive to expand AI chip production. The two hyperscalers were already gaining ground in securing supply-chain capacity relative to Nvidia, Patel said, and could accelerate those efforts without Huang's influence over suppliers. "If Nvidia can't muster the supply chain, then technology is the only competitive advantage. And without Jensen, can they maintain technology advantages? Given they're only a year ahead of their biggest competitors, it's not like the gap is massive," Patel said. The challenge is particularly acute as hyperscalers increasingly develop proprietary AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, while AMD and other semiconductor companies race to capture a larger slice of the market. Yet the upheaval doesn't necessarily signal an end to the broader AI investment boom. Franklin noted that major technology companies are projecting higher AI spending in 2027, with further increases possible in 2028, signaling the investment cycle remains structurally intact even as investors reassess which companies stand to benefit. The bigger question is whether growing competition and the proliferation of open-source technologies eventually commoditize AI capabilities, putting pressure on chip prices and investment returns, he said. For Nvidia, the immediate outlook may depend less on its earnings than on whether its next leadership team can reassure investors. Azam said the stock appeared inexpensive relative to its earnings growth prospects, but warned that ongoing investigations and management uncertainty could limit any sustained recovery. He expects Nvidia's earnings due Nov. 17 to remain strong, with investors likely to focus more closely on management's plans for navigating the crisis. The result could be a reshuffling of winners within the semiconductor industry, with Franklin saying that investors were becoming more comfortable staying invested while rotating and diversifying their portfolios, instead of abandoning the market altogether.
ranking_reason: Leadership crisis at Nvidia may impact the broader AI investment boom and create opportunities for other chipmakers

analysis.reason: Leadership crisis at Nvidia may impact the broader AI investment boom and create opportunities for other chipmakers

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant development in the science and technology category, specifically in the field of AI and chip design, with tangible implications for investors and the industry. The article provides a clear reason for readers to care, namely the potential for a shift in market momentum and opportunities for alternative chipmakers to gain traction. The analysis is supported by quotes from market watchers and industry experts, providing a trusted source of information.
